doc.title: Ray Ricker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 27, 2022

title: Saxophone study in the 1960s and becoming Eastman's first Professor of Saxophone
summary: Few schools offered sax degrees; Ricker was the first with the professor title and taught sax to jazz and classical students.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: It’s rather stunning, the state of jazz education how it just sort of exploded over the years and now it’s an integral part of almost any music school across the country.

Yeah, it is. And also, the saxophone. I’ll tell you, in the 1960s there were not many places you could study saxophone and get a degree. Joe Farrell — Monk, you know his name I know, Joe Farrell who played with Corea and had a good career as a solo saxophone © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
player. He was a flute major at Illinois. They didn’t have saxophone. He couldn’t major in saxophone, it was in flute.
In fact, weren’t you the first saxophone professor at Eastman?

Yes. Well the first one with that title. There was a person teaching there who was on the clarinet faculty who also had several students — not many but a few, you know. And his name was Bill Ossick and he taught that. But I was the first one that had the title of Professor of Saxophone.
And it was mostly classical I would imagine? Is that correct?

It was, but they still had to take classical juries. But what we did, we did a lot of jazz you know. And many of those players from that period are extremely successful professional musicians. It didn’t hurt them one bit. But then we got the master’s degree doing. And there was straight jazz. And then after that came the bachelor’s of jazz performance, or jazz composition. And so now we had these kind of two strings, or two streams, but I always just tried to teach the saxophone and then allow the students to decide what kind of music they wanted to play.
